OK, LSJ, I searched this newsgroup, and I'm surprised I couldn't find
the answers to these questions. Here we go:

1.) I bring out Marie Faucigny (cause I like doing that.) My
grandprey brings out Ingrid Rossler, contesting the Geneva title. On
my turn, I pay to contest, and then I draw into a Cardinal
Benediction. I call it on Marie, it passes--am I no longer
contesting? Or may I continue to pay to contest the archbishop title
(because it is not in play), gaining (and yielding) one of my titles
when Ingrid gives in?

2.) I play Major Boon on my grandprey when he's being bled for six,
because I have a Protected Resources in play. Am I:
--smart, because I can't be bled for more than 2 pool?
--pretty dumb, because the vampire is bleeding someone else, even
though I'm losing the pool for it?

That's all, thanks.

-- Brian

No title to contest means no more contesting.

>
> 2.) I play Major Boon on my grandprey when he's being bled for six,
> because I have a Protected Resources in play. Am I:
> --smart, because I can't be bled for more than 2 pool?
> --pretty dumb, because the vampire is bleeding someone else, even

relevant parts of card text:
PR: ...'You do not burn more than 2 pool when a minion bleeds *you*'...

does nothing.

> contesting? Or may I continue to pay to contest the archbishop title
> (because it is not in play), gaining (and yielding) one of my titles
> when Ingrid gives in?

When you gain a new title you automatically yield all contests of the
old title. Marie would become the Cardinal and Ingrid would gain her
Prince of Geneva title in her controller's next untap phase.

> 2.) I play Major Boon on my grandprey when he's being bled for six,
> because I have a Protected Resources in play. Am I:
> --smart, because I can't be bled for more than 2 pool?
> --pretty dumb, because the vampire is bleeding someone else, even
> though I'm losing the pool for it?

Pretty dumb because the target of the bleed is the methuselah you play
Major Boon on and Protected Resources protects only against bleeds
targetting you.

So I am able to have one title, regardless of whether one of the
titles is contested. Does this apply to other things you can only
have one of?

Example: If I have a vampire contesting the haven Zaire River Ferry,
who I equip with a Body Bag, do I have to give up the Zaire River
Ferry (since I can have only 1 haven)? Or do I still "have" a haven
the way Marie still "has" a title, prohibiting me from getting a new
haven anyway?

Also, let's say instead of Cardinal Benediction, Marie (still
contesting Geneva with Ingrid) calls and passes Crusade: Miami while
Gilbert Duane is in play. Does she immediately give up contesting
Geneva in order to contest Miami? Or give up Miami in order to
contest Geneva? By strict wording of section 10 in the rulebook --
which I should have read before starting this thread -- she should
give up both titles, since both are contested, but I don't think that
makes sense.

> So I am able to have one title, regardless of whether one of the

Correct.
http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/rulebook/rulebook.html#sec10

> Does this apply to other things you can only
> have one of?
>
> Example: If I have a vampire contesting the haven Zaire River Ferry,
> who I equip with a Body Bag, do I have to give up the Zaire River
> Ferry (since I can have only 1 haven)? Or do I still "have" a haven
> the way Marie still "has" a title, prohibiting me from getting a new
> haven anyway?

The contested haven is out of play, so doesn't count as having a haven.
If the contest is won, one of the havens will have to be burned (controller's
choice).

Similarly, if an Ahrimane has a contested Mr. Winthrop, and she then gets the
Wildebeest, Mr. Winthrop will remain contested. If the Ahrimane's controller
wins the contest, the Mr. Winthrop will burn when he comes back into play, due
to the Wildebeest's card text.

> Also, let's say instead of Cardinal Benediction, Marie (still
> contesting Geneva with Ingrid) calls and passes Crusade: Miami while
> Gilbert Duane is in play. Does she immediately give up contesting
> Geneva in order to contest Miami?

Yes (card text).

> contest Geneva? By strict wording of section 10 in the rulebook --
> which I should have read before starting this thread -- she should
> give up both titles, since both are contested, but I don't think that
> makes sense.

A strict reading of section 10 does not suggest both are lost.

Messages.Author: islando...@aol.com
Messages.Body:
> > Also, let's say instead of Cardinal Benediction, Marie (still
> > contesting Geneva with Ingrid) calls and passes Crusade: Miami while
> > Gilbert Duane is in play. Does she immediately give up contesting
> > Geneva in order to contest Miami?
>
> Yes (card text).

Relevant Card Text:
"This could lead to a contested title."

Your "Yes" alone strikes me as a perfectly good answer, but I don't
see how the card text would lead me to the idea that contesting a
title would cause me to cease contesting another title. It may feel
like an intuitive answer, but it is certainly not printed in the
textbox.

> > Or give up Miami in order to
> > contest Geneva? By strict wording of section 10 in the rulebook --
> > which I should have read before starting this thread -- she should
> > give up both titles, since both are contested, but I don't think that
> > makes sense.
>
> A strict reading of section 10 does not suggest both are lost.

Section 10 reads in part:
If a vampire with a contested title (see Contested Titles, sec. 4.2)
gains a title, he immediately yields the contested title.

So, strictly speaking, in the above example where Marie is contesting
Geneva and becomes Archbishop of Miami:
-- She is a vampire with a contested title
-- She gained a title
-- She must relinquish the contested title.

Both of her titles are contested, so she must relinquish the one which
is contested. Which in this case matches both.

Now, I know that the sentence in the rulebook is referential text,
rather like Jimmy Dunn's referential text ("burn the first Jimmy").
What I mean specifically is that I understand that the phrase "the
contested title" does not mean whichever title happens to be
contested, but rather "the contested title we were just talking
about". So in English, she burns the title referenced earlier in the
sentence, but strictly literally speaking, she yields "the contested
title", which is either or both.

I understand how the rule works, I think, and I don't suppose anyone
could interpret the rule this literal way unless they were trying to
be difficult--I was just pointing out that technically, if you only
use logical rules and not English grammar, you come out with one or
both titles being yielded.

I probably wouldn't have mentioned it, except for the ruling years ago
on some Necromancy card which returns an ally to play not being able
to return Jake Washington, because he's not an ally in the discard
pile, although by English rules where words can reference previous
parts of the sentence, I felt the ruling was logical but not based on
English rules of grammar.

I guess its a desire for all cards to either follow English rules of
grammar, or be strictly literal and logical, as I don't think they can
always be both, and I don't want to have to guess when LSJ is allowing
text to refer back to previous sentences and when he's not.

-- Brian

Then we agree standard English should be used over another
interpretation, meaning "the contested title" refers to the previously-
mentioned title.

Similarly, on Compel the Spirit, standard English should be used,
meaning "the ally" refers to the previously-mentioned ally.

Remember the change in Ian Forestal's interaction with Infernal
Familiar? "If he does so" used to mean, literally, "if he plays a
card which requires a discipline he does not have," so using his
ability would put counters on the Infernal Familiar. Later, Infernal
Familiar was reinterpreted to be self-referential: If he does so (as
previously mentioned), put a counter on the Familiar.

It's not really that important for normal gameplay (how often do you
want an Infernal Familiar on Forestal anyway?) but technically I think
it's better for text which is worded in a self-referential manner to
function as such.

> > I probably wouldn't have mentioned it, except for the ruling years ago
> > on some Necromancy card which returns an ally to play not being able
> > to return Jake Washington, because he's not an ally in the discard
> > pile, although by English rules where words can reference previous
> > parts of the sentence, I felt the ruling was logical but not based on
> > English rules of grammar.
>
> It still works there. He's not an ally in the ash heap.

If Compel the Spirit said "move the ally card," then I think that
statement would be relevant. But since it does not--it merely says
"move the card", referencing the previous "ally or retainer who was
burned"--it has to be assumed that the reference means "move [the ally
or retainer which was burned since your last turn]" into your hand/
into play at basic/superior. It does happen to specify that it has to
be a card, but it does not specify that it had to be an ally or a
retainer at any point other than when it was being burned. If the
card "Jake Washington" was an ally who died since my last turn, then
it's just an application of English over card text to determine that
moving "the card" to play moves "the Jake Washington card" from my ash
heap to play.

> > I guess its a desire for all cards to either follow English rules of
> > grammar, or be strictly literal and logical, as I don't think they can
> > always be both, and I don't want to have to guess when LSJ is allowing
> > text to refer back to previous sentences and when he's not.
>
> That's fine. No guessing needed here.
> Just follow English grammar all the time.

So, since we're in agreement that English grammar should determine
cards' functions based on their texts, instead of some other way of
reading them, then all we would need is some way of determining what
way that sentence structure functions. I personally think the
precedents above are enough, but you disagree, so let's see if there's
a reasonable source for understanding English.

What would it take to convince you that Compel the Spirit is ruled
differently from the way it is worded? I would gladly go ask a random
sample of native English speakers, or a random sample of English
professors, or just all of the local English professors, or whatever
you would accept as "sufficient" in order to determine this issue one
way or the other, and if the results came up in favor of your way OR
came up inconclusive, I would be willing to concede the point.

I will seriously go do this if you tell me what sample of the populace
you think would be appropriate to ask in order to determine the
"proper" function of the sentence in question.

-- Brian
